---
title: "Near a Hospital, Near a Pharmacy?"
subtitle: "Two perspectives on geographic proximity to healthcare facilities"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
    theme: cosmo
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

health <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-29/health.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

access_comparison <- health |>
  transmute(
    city = gc_ucn_mai_2025,
    country = gc_cnt_gad_2025,
    population = gc_pop_tot_2025,
    hospital_pct = hl_shp_hos_2025,
    pharmacy_pct = hl_shp_pha_2025
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(hospital_pct),
    !is.na(pharmacy_pct)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hospital_advantage_pp = hospital_pct - pharmacy_pct
  )
```

## Story summary

Does living near one type of healthcare facility imply living near another?
Among 2,345 urban centres with both proximity measurements available,
the median share of residents living within one kilometre of a hospital
is 31.8%, compared with 18.8% for a pharmacy.

However, comparing these separate medians does not establish whether
the hospital advantage holds within individual cities. A paired
comparison shows that hospital proximity is higher in 68.7% of urban
centres, while pharmacy proximity is higher in 717 cities and the two
measures are equal in 18. The median within-city difference is 9.47
percentage points in favour of hospitals.

The story therefore progresses from an overall contrast to an important
qualification: hospital proximity is usually higher, but not everywhere.
Proximity to one facility type should not be assumed to indicate
equivalent proximity to another.

These findings describe the subset of urban centres with both
measurements available. They measure geographic proximity, not
healthcare quality, affordability, capacity, or actual use.

## Version A: Scientific article

### Comparing the distributions

Hospital and pharmacy proximity describe different aspects of geographic
access. We first compare their distributions across the same 2,345 urban
centres, giving each urban centre equal weight.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scientific-distributions
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: "Two greyscale histograms compare hospital and pharmacy proximity across 2,345 urban centres. Dashed lines mark median proximity of 31.8 percent for hospitals and 18.8 percent for pharmacies."
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of population proximity to hospitals and pharmacies in the matched sample. Each observation is an urban centre; bars represent 5-percentage-point intervals. Dashed lines indicate medians. Both panels use identical scales."

access_long_final <- access_comparison |>
  select(hospital_pct, pharmacy_pct) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "facility",
    values_to = "proximity_pct"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    facility = factor(
      facility,
      levels = c("hospital_pct", "pharmacy_pct"),
      labels = c("Hospital", "Pharmacy")
    )
  )

median_labels <- access_long_final |>
  group_by(facility) |>
  summarise(
    median_pct = median(proximity_pct),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    label = paste0("Median: ", round(median_pct, 1), "%")
  )

scientific_1 <- ggplot(
  access_long_final,
  aes(x = proximity_pct)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "grey75",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = median_labels,
    aes(xintercept = median_pct),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = median_labels,
    aes(x = 98, y = Inf, label = label),
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 3.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ facility, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "Residents living within 1 km of the facility (%)",
    y = "Number of urban centres"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95")
  )

print(scientific_1)
```

Median hospital proximity is 31.8%, compared with 18.8% for pharmacies.
These are medians of city-level population shares, not estimates for the
combined population of all sampled cities.

However, separate distributions cannot establish how often hospital
proximity exceeds pharmacy proximity within the same city. We therefore
turn to a paired comparison.

### Comparing facilities within cities

For each urban centre, we subtract pharmacy proximity from hospital
proximity. A positive difference indicates higher hospital proximity;
a negative difference indicates higher pharmacy proximity. Differences
are expressed in percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scientific-differences
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-alt: "A greyscale histogram shows within-city differences in hospital minus pharmacy proximity. Hospital proximity is higher in 1,610 cities, pharmacy proximity is higher in 717, and 18 have equal proximity. The median difference is 9.47 percentage points."
#| fig-cap: "Within-city differences in population proximity to hospitals and pharmacies among 2,345 urban centres. Bars represent 5-percentage-point intervals. The solid vertical line marks equal proximity; the dashed line marks the median difference of 9.47 percentage points. Eighteen urban centres have equal proximity."

scientific_2 <- ggplot(
  access_comparison,
  aes(x = hospital_advantage_pp)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "grey75",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(
      access_comparison$hospital_advantage_pp
    ),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = -95,
    y = Inf,
    label = "Pharmacy proximity higher\n717 urban centres",
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1.2,
    size = 3.3
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = 95,
    y = Inf,
    label = "Hospital proximity higher\n1,610 urban centres",
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 1.2,
    size = 3.3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-100, 100, 25)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(-100, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hospital proximity minus pharmacy proximity (percentage points)",
    y = "Number of urban centres"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(scientific_2)
```

Hospital proximity exceeds pharmacy proximity in 1,610 of the 2,345
urban centres (68.7%). Pharmacy proximity is higher in 717 urban centres,
while 18 have equal proximity. The median within-city difference is
9.47 percentage points in favour of hospitals.

The paired comparison qualifies the initial distributional contrast:
the hospital advantage is common, but not universal. Moreover, the
median paired difference is not the difference between the two
separate medians. Each paired difference compares the two facility
types within the same urban centre.

These findings are descriptive and apply to the matched available-data
sample. They do not establish a causal relationship or measure healthcare
quality, capacity, affordability, or utilization.

## Version B: Accessible explainer

### More residents live near hospitals in the typical city

A hospital and a pharmacy serve different needs. Being geographically
close to one does not necessarily mean being close to the other.

We compared the share of residents living within one kilometre of each
facility type in 2,345 urban centres with both measurements available.
In the typical city in this sample, the hospital percentage is higher.

```{r}
#| label: fig-accessible-medians
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bars show median population proximity: 31.8 percent for hospitals and 18.8 percent for pharmacies. Facility names and percentages are directly labelled."
#| fig-cap: "Median city-level proximity in the same 2,345 urban centres. These percentages do not describe the combined population of the sampled cities."

public_medians <- access_comparison |>
  summarise(
    Hospital = median(hospital_pct),
    Pharmacy = median(pharmacy_pct)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "facility",
    values_to = "median_pct"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    facility = factor(
      facility,
      levels = c("Pharmacy", "Hospital")
    ),
    value_label = paste0(
      round(median_pct, 1),
      "%"
    )
  )

accessible_1 <- ggplot(
  public_medians,
  aes(
    x = median_pct,
    y = facility,
    fill = facility
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = value_label),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Hospital" = "#0072B2",
      "Pharmacy" = "#D55E00"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "About 32% near hospitals, versus 19% near pharmacies",
    subtitle = "Median share of residents living within 1 km",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(
      size = 13,
      colour = "black"
    ),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )

print(accessible_1)
```

“Typical” here means the median urban centre: half the cities have
proximity at or below that value, and half at or above it. Each city
counts equally, regardless of population.

But these two summary values leave something unresolved. Does hospital
proximity exceed pharmacy proximity within most individual cities—or
does the overall comparison hide a different city-by-city pattern?

### But the hospital advantage is not universal

To answer that question, we compared hospital and pharmacy proximity
within each city. The hospital advantage holds in about seven out of
ten urban centres—but there are hundreds of exceptions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-accessible-comparison
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-alt: "Three directly labelled horizontal bars show that hospital proximity is higher in 68.7 percent of urban centres, pharmacy proximity is higher in 30.6 percent, and proximity is equal in 0.8 percent."
#| fig-cap: "Within-city comparison for 2,345 urban centres with both measurements available. Percentages describe cities, not the combined population. Rounded percentages may not total exactly 100%."

public_comparison <- access_comparison |>
  mutate(
    outcome = case_when(
      hospital_advantage_pp > 0 ~ "Hospital proximity higher",
      hospital_advantage_pp < 0 ~ "Pharmacy proximity higher",
      TRUE ~ "Equal proximity"
    )
  ) |>
  count(outcome, name = "cities") |>
  mutate(
    percent = 100 * cities / sum(cities),
    outcome = factor(
      outcome,
      levels = c(
        "Equal proximity",
        "Pharmacy proximity higher",
        "Hospital proximity higher"
      )
    ),
    value_label = paste0(
      round(percent, 1),
      "%  (",
      scales::comma(cities),
      " cities)"
    )
  )

accessible_2 <- ggplot(
  public_comparison,
  aes(
    x = percent,
    y = outcome,
    fill = outcome
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = value_label),
    hjust = -0.12,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Hospital proximity higher" = "#0072B2",
      "Pharmacy proximity higher" = "#D55E00",
      "Equal proximity" = "#666666"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Hospitals have the advantage—but not everywhere",
    subtitle = "Pharmacy proximity is higher in 717 urban centres",
    x = "Share of urban centres",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(
      size = 11,
      colour = "black"
    ),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )

print(accessible_2)
```

Hospital proximity is higher in 1,610 cities, while pharmacy proximity
is higher in 717. The remaining 18 have equal proximity.

How large is the difference? Across the matched sample, the median
hospital-minus-pharmacy gap is 9.47 percentage points. For example,
40% near a hospital and 30% near a pharmacy would represent a
10-percentage-point hospital advantage. This example illustrates the
unit; it is not a reported city measurement.

The takeaway is not that hospitals are always easier to reach. It is
that the two kinds of geographic proximity are not interchangeable:
a city can score differently depending on which facility type we examine.

Finally, “within one kilometre” does not tell us whether a facility is
affordable, adequately staffed, or accessible along actual travel routes.
These findings describe geographic proximity in the available-data
sample, not the overall adequacy of healthcare.

## Data and source note

### Source and measurement

This analysis uses `health.csv` from the
[TidyTuesday release of 29 September 2026](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2026/2026-09-29/readme.md).
The underlying source is the European Commission Joint Research Centre's
Global Human Settlement Urban Centre Database, GHS-UCDB R2024A:
GHS Urban Centre Database 2025.

The unit of analysis is an urban centre as delineated in that database,
not necessarily an administrative municipality.

The analysis uses two indicators:

- `HL_SHP_HOS_2025`: share of the urban-centre population living within a 1 km buffer of a hospital.
- `HL_SHP_PHA_2025`: share living within a 1 km buffer of a pharmacy.

In the supplied CSV, these values are expressed on a 0–100 percentage
scale. They are not multiplied by 100 during analysis.

### Analytical sample and missing values

The dataset contains 11,422 urban centres. Hospital proximity is missing
for 4,988 and pharmacy proximity for 8,952. These missingness counts
overlap.

The analysis retains the 2,345 urban centres with both proximity
measurements available—approximately one-fifth of the original dataset.
The same matched sample is used throughout both presentation versions.
Missing values are excluded, not interpreted as zero proximity.
Income-group information and city names are not required for inclusion.

The reasons for missingness are not established in this analysis.
The retained cities may differ systematically from excluded cities.
Consequently, these results should not be treated as representative
estimates for all urban centres worldwide.

### Calculations and interpretation

Each urban centre receives equal weight. The medians and comparison
percentages therefore describe cities, not the combined population
of all cities.

For each city, the paired difference is calculated as:

**Hospital proximity − pharmacy proximity**

A positive difference indicates higher hospital proximity; a negative
difference indicates higher pharmacy proximity. Differences are measured
in percentage points.

The median paired difference is calculated from the individual
city-level differences. It is not calculated by subtracting the two
separate facility medians.

Both scientific histograms use 5-percentage-point intervals. The
accessible figures summarize the same sample using facility medians
and the proportions of cities with positive, negative, or zero
differences. Displayed values are rounded.

### Limitations

A one-kilometre buffer measures geographic proximity. It does not measure
travel time, route accessibility, affordability, staffing, service
capacity, healthcare quality, or actual utilization.

Hospitals and pharmacies provide different services. Higher proximity
to one facility type is not evidence that it substitutes for the other
or that a city's healthcare provision is adequate.

The analysis is descriptive. No causal effects or population-level
inferential claims are estimated. No confidence intervals are presented:
the figures summarize the available-data sample, and uncertainty about
coverage and missingness is not resolved by these descriptive summaries.

## Generative AI disclosure

I used Perplexity, a generative AI assistant, to support this assignment.
AI assistance contributed initial exploration of dataset;
development of the narrative; R code for data import,
cleaning, descriptive calculations, and visualization; interpretation
of summary results; and preparation of the Quarto document.

I requested help adapting the same empirical story for scientific and
public-facing audiences, drafting and revising the story summary,
explanatory prose, figure captions, accessibility text, and data/source
note. I also requested step-by-step RStudio and Quarto guidance and
troubleshooting of package compatibility, percentage scaling,
missing variables, plot labelling, axis limits, and document rendering.

The assistance included proposed code and text that I incorporated
into the deliverable, rather than only editing material I had written.
I ran the code and inspected the resulting outputs. Some initial
AI-generated suggestions and code required correction during the
workflow.

The AI Prompt Appendix reproduces the prompts used in this work
verbatim. The complete conversation, including responses and supplied
screenshots, is retained for instructor or TA review.
